summary.summary: Worcestershire's borrowing jumped £118.1m in 2025/26 to £725.2m — including £221.2m of new PWLB — as internal borrowing collapsed from £123.9m to £27.7m and was replaced with external debt, and short-term borrowing more than doubled to £225.2m, deliberately breaching the council's own 25% under-one-year maturity limit (31.1% actual) rather than lock in long-term rates it hopes will fall. Year-end liquidity is thin: net cash and investments of £16.3m against the £725.2m debt pile, with the bank account £27.6m overdrawn at 31 March (gross money-market and bond fund holdings were £52.7m, including fire authority monies, 99% accessible within 28 days). The report also discloses a £180.8m negative DSG schools reserve 'impacting the resource-base of the balance sheet', and the council rates the current treasury risk HIGH (residual medium). Net treasury costs still came in £6.4m under budget at £31.8m.

signals.headline: Total external borrowing rose £118.1m in 2025/26, from £607.1m to £725.2m, including £221.2m of new PWLB; internal borrowing unwound from £123.9m to £27.7m
signals.why: A structural shift from internal resources to external debt enlarges the interest bill (£22.3m paid this year) and puts borrowing of £716.9m close under the £750m authorised limit.

signals.headline: £225.2m (31.1% of debt) matures within 12 months at 31 March 2026, above the council's own 0-25% indicator limit — a breach it accepted deliberately; short-term borrowing more than doubled from £110.5m in the year
signals.why: The council is betting that Middle-East-driven rates fall before the rollovers bite, and £104.3m of local-authority loans with 0.7-year average maturity must be continuously refinanced meanwhile.

signals.headline: Negative DSG reserve of £180.8m at 31 March 2026, which the report says is impacting the resource-base of the balance sheet
signals.why: A £180.8m hole behind the statutory override drains the internal balances that previously substituted for external borrowing.

signals.headline: Net cash and investments of £16.3m at 31 March 2026 against £725.2m of borrowing, with bank balances overdrawn by £27.6m at year end
signals.why: Day-to-day resilience depends on continuous access to short-term markets, mitigated by £52.7m of gross fund holdings (including fire authority monies) that are 99% accessible within 28 days.

signals.headline: Deliberately exceeded its own 25% short-maturity limit — short-term debt doubled to £225.2m (31.1% of £725.2m)
signals.why: A council that answers a limit breach by tolerating it weakens the guardrail lenders price on.

compliance.notes: Re-scored the 2026/27 TMSS (Appendix 4, s59998) together with the standalone Capital Strategy 2026-29 (Appendix 5, s59999), a county council under Exceptional Financial Support with no HRA. Strongest areas are the core prudential/treasury mechanics: a full year-on-year CFR reconciliation, a transparent gross-debt-vs-CFR position that explicitly flags the planned DSG-driven short-term breach, an exemplary liability benchmark charted to 2089 with all four balances and a liquidity buffer, an SLY-driven MUFG creditworthiness/counterparty framework, an integrated borrowing strategy explaining the under-borrowed position, and a well-disclosed asset-life MRP policy with the VRP overpayment position. The capital strategy adds the capital-strategy, due-diligence and broader risk-framework content. Weakest areas remain the commercial/non-treasury disclosures (proportionality asserted but not quantified; net-commercial-income indicator, IMPs, statutory security/income-dependence disclosures, exit review and service/commercial limits each only referenced, not delivered), the absence of any audit-qualification flag on source data (notable under EFS with delayed accounts), and thin third-party/pension-monies and derivatives coverage.

gaps.evidence: TMSS p.3-4 lists the PC requirement for a prudential indicator on net commercial/service income to net revenue stream
TMSS p.4 references PC para 51 (must not borrow to invest primarily for financial return) as content to include

Capital Strategy s.6 (CFO ensures proportionality vs financial resources) and s.9 (proportionality of proposals vs overall resources); TMSS p.2-3 plausible-losses-absorbed-in-reserves test; TMSS p.22 CFO proportionality responsibility
TMSS p.3 notes the requirement to create Investment Management Practices for non-treasury investments

TMSS p.22 Table 16 fair value (Malvern Hills £1.5m fair value vs £4.4m cost); Capital Strategy s.6 (additional risks/sustainability impact set out) and s.19 (credit risk, contingency plans identified at outset)
TMSS p.3 notes the PC requires an annual review of whether commercial investments should be sold to release funds; Capital Strategy s.13.2 capital receipts may repay debt

news_drafts.headline: Worcestershire forecasts £131.6m schools grant deficit at March 2027, up from £122.2m at quarter 1
news_drafts.lead:
Worcestershire County Council forecasts that its cumulative deficit on the dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools, will reach £131.6m at 31 March 2027. The quarter 1 forecast was £122.2m. For 31 March 2028 the forecast is £170.0m, against £150.1m at quarter 1. The figures are in budget presentation slides for the council's Corporate and Communities Overview and Scrutiny Panel, which meets on 7 December.

The slides set the deficit against the high needs grant, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. The council expects £102.2m of it for 2026/27, compared with £93.7m expected at quarter 1. They also refer to the end of the statutory override during 2027/28. That is a temporary government rule that lets councils keep a schools-funding deficit off their main balance sheet.

The slides forecast a £3.7m overspend on the council's Financing Transactions budgets for 2026/27, "due to increased borrowing costs associated with the council's high needs deficit". The quarter 1 forecast was a £5.4m overspend, so the figure is down £1.6m. The paper attributes the reduction to further reprofiling of the capital programme and to interest on lending.

news_drafts.headline: Worcestershire's 2026/27 budget balanced with £59.9m of exceptional support; £35m–£40m needed for 2027/28
news_drafts.lead:
Worcestershire County Council balanced its 2026/27 budget with £59.9m of exceptional financial support, which is government permission to borrow to cover day-to-day spending, and an 8.98% council tax increase. Its Audit and Governance Committee on 4 December was told the corporate risk for financial instability has been rated red, with a current and anticipated score of 25, since August 2023.

For 2027/28, the council's action tracker sets out that a reduction, savings or income generation of "c. £35m–£40m" would be required if the support is to be no higher than in 2026/27. The Senior Leadership Team and Cabinet are preparing the budget. Cabinet meets on 17 December 2026 and 13 January 2027 to consider proposals, ahead of a Council meeting on 14 January 2027. The council's budget paper says any demand pressure not met by income increases or savings would be met through the support, which central government must approve. That borrowing is added to the council's debt and must be repaid.

The budget timetable estimates confirmation of the support on 18 February 2027. Cabinet on 23 February and Council on 25 February are to approve the budget "subject to receiving the EFS approval". Council on 4 March 2027 is reserved if approval has not arrived. The council's papers say the Government's ministry (MHCLG) assurance review of progress in paying back the support required a response by 30 September 2026. External audit's first key recommendation asks the council to reduce reliance on the support and its "very limited reserves", and to agree a reserves replenishment plan.

news_drafts.headline: Worcestershire's 2026/27 budget includes £59.9m of exceptional financial support, unchanged since quarter 1
news_drafts.lead:
Worcestershire County Council's 2026/27 budget includes £59.9m of exceptional financial support, the same sum as at the end of the first quarter. The figure appears in the period 6 (quarter 2) budget monitoring slides before the Children and Families Overview and Scrutiny Panel, which meets on 3 December 2026. Exceptional financial support is government permission to borrow, or sell assets, to cover day-to-day spending.

The papers give the line as £59.933m, with no change and a 0.0% variance against the period 3 position. The support is applied to the budget as a capitalisation directive, which is government permission to treat day-to-day spending as capital spending so that borrowing can pay for it. The paper explains that borrowing to cover day-to-day spending is not allowed in this form without the approval of the Secretary of State. It says the support reflects pressures in adult and children's social care.

The same slides put the total capital programme at £574.5m, against £574.3m at quarter 1. They give borrowing of £168.8m, against £166.0m at quarter 1.

findings.committee: Corporate and Communities Overview and Scrutiny Panel
findings.headline: The County Museum's new business model begins in 2026/27, with Hartlebury Castle Preservation Trust setting admission prices, and the council says the transition will not affect the 2026/27 operational budget.
findings.detail: The Trust controls site marketing and visit monitoring under the new operating model. The council says it will still offer free and subsidised programming through externally funded grants. The paper says comparisons with earlier years are not meaningful because of the change.
findings.matters: Transferring a museum's operating model and pricing to a third-party trust, with the council reporting that the operational budget is unaffected, is a service-change structure other councils consider.
findings.figures: 5,025 people participating in activities in the first six months; 2,240 take-up of formal and informal learning; 3,548 September visits to the North Wing
findings.quote: The transition to the new business model for the County Museum will not impact on 2026/2027’s operational budget.

findings.committee: Corporate and Communities Overview and Scrutiny Panel
findings.headline: The Bikeability Trust provided significantly less Level 1 funding in 2026/27, and the council's Level 1 allocation was exhausted within the first two quarters.
findings.detail: The council has stopped actively promoting Level 1 training to new schools and is seeking to reduce its volume. The paper says the summer holiday and Saturday programmes, partly funded through the Bikeability Trust's Inclusion funding, were expanded, and a fourth venue is planned.
findings.matters: A grant-funder cut that exhausts an allocation mid-year, leading to a reduced service, is a funding-dependency risk that other councils running grant-funded training will recognise.
findings.figures: Level 1 allocation exhausted within the first two quarters; Level 2 target of 800 children per quarter; other levels target of 730 children per quarter
findings.quote: The Bikeability Trust provided significantly less funding for Level 1 Bikeability this year compared with previous years.

findings.committee: Corporate and Communities Overview and Scrutiny Panel
findings.headline: Sickness absence in April to September 2026 totalled 10,360 days lost, which the paper reports as 4.9% above the same period of 2025.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the increase partly to the October 2024 re-integration of Children's Services staff. It says long-term absence of 21 days or more is driving the higher figure, with psychological, musculoskeletal and stress as the top three reasons. Long-term absence days in 2025/26 were 10.9% lower than in 2024/25.
findings.matters: Sickness days drive cover costs and agency demand, and the paper separates the re-integration effect from the underlying long-term absence trend.
findings.figures: 10,360 days lost April-September 2026; 9,877 days April-September 2025 (+4.9%); 4.36 days per FTE cumulative at mid-year; 7.72 days per FTE 2025/26 full year; 8 days per FTE target
findings.quote: The total of 10,360 days lost in the first half of this financial year was 483 (4.9%) higher

findings.committee: Corporate and Communities Overview and Scrutiny Panel
findings.headline: Staff turnover at 30 September 2026 was 4.23%, the lowest 30 September percentage in three years.
findings.detail: The paper reports turnover 1.61 percentage points below the April-to-September 2025 figure of 5.84%. It rates the measure green against a 14% annual turnover target, and says the 2025/26 out-turn was 9.88%. The paper also notes increased retirements, with 35% of the workforce aged 55 or over.
findings.matters: Lower turnover reduces recruitment and training costs, and a multi-year low is a measurable change in workforce stability that peers can benchmark.
findings.figures: 4.23% turnover at 30 September 2026; 5.84% April-September 2025 (1.61 percentage points lower); 14% annual target; 9.88% 2025/26 out-turn; 3.46% voluntary resignations turnover
findings.quote: being 4.23%, the lowest 30th September percentage for three years

findings.committee: Corporate and Communities Overview and Scrutiny Panel
findings.headline: The paper says the council's financial situation and Local Government Reorganisation decisions have created more uncertainty for its employees, and that this may affect turnover.
findings.detail: The paper's turnover section links the council's finances and LGR to a possible rise in staff leaving for organisations seen as more stable. Earlier in the same paper, the council describes scrutiny of resources as creating anxiety for employees.
findings.matters: A council citing its own financial position as a retention risk is a signal finance directors and lenders may weigh alongside other workforce and budget indicators.
findings.quote: The financial situation of the Council and the Local Government Reorganisation decisions have created more uncertainty for County Council employees.
